passage: Campaign statement: On Tuesday my opponent's campaign called me 'a trust-fund kid who's never worked a day.' That's a personal attack, and it says nothing about my housing plan. I'm happy to debate the plan anytime, and I've proposed three dates.

Product page: In a 6-month study of 9,000 users, people who used our SleepWell app fell asleep an average of 4 minutes faster than those who didn't, a statistically significant difference (p < 0.001). Few sleep products have been tested on this many people. In other words, users can expect a significant improvement in their nights. Try it free for 30 days.

Hospital data brief: Patients seen by our palliative-care team had a 90-day mortality of 41%, compared with 9% for all other inpatients. The numbers come from 5,000 admissions and are not in dispute. Families should think carefully before agreeing to a palliative referral. We also found that palliative patients reported higher satisfaction with communication.

Prosecution closing: The forensic analyst testified, and the defense did not dispute, that the chance of a random unrelated person matching the crime-scene DNA profile is one in a million. The sample was handled properly at every step. In other words, there is roughly a one-in-a-million chance that the defendant is innocent. That is proof beyond any reasonable doubt.

Evaluation memo: The state phased in automatic prescription-drug monitoring county by county between 2019 and 2022. Opioid overdose admissions fell after rollout. A simple before-and-after comparison would prove little. But in each of the six counties, the drop began within two months of that county's own start date, and it did not appear in neighboring counties that had not yet adopted the program. That pattern is hard to explain by statewide trends or chance, so we attribute most of the decline to the program.

History feature: Opponents warned in 2004 that if same-sex couples could marry, 'people will be marrying their dogs next.' Logic teachers now use the line as a stock example of a slippery-slope argument. The article traces how the phrase spread through talk radio that year.

Press conference. REPORTER: Your own monitoring wells show trichloroethylene above the federal limit at the fence line. Is the plant contaminating the groundwater? SPOKESPERSON: This plant employs 1,100 people in this county and has paid $40 million in local taxes since 2015. We sponsor the youth soccer league and the food bank. We are proud to be a good neighbor.

Education memo: A national survey of 20,000 teenagers found that those who ate dinner with their families five or more nights a week had GPAs 0.4 points higher than those who rarely did. The association held across racial groups. If we want to close achievement gaps, the district should require each school to run a family-dinner campaign. Materials would cost under $3 per student.

Public-health memo: The rapid screen is accurate in the lab, but the condition is rare in the general population. With 1% prevalence, 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity, only about 16% of positive results will be true positives. A positive screen should therefore trigger a confirmatory test, not treatment. Clinics should tell patients this before testing so a positive result doesn't cause needless alarm.

Watchdog post: Every charity fraud we've investigated in the past decade spent more than 40% of its budget on fundraising and paid its director more than $300,000. These are the numbers to watch. The Hope Bridge Foundation also spends over 40% of its budget on fundraising and pays its director more than $300,000, so donors should treat it as a likely fraud. Give your money somewhere else this year.

Floor speech: Border crossings hit a record last year, and the agencies say they lack the staff to process claims. This bill adds 1,500 officers and funds 22 new immigration judges, both of which I support. Either we pass this bill as written, or we are choosing to leave the border open. I urge my colleagues to vote yes.

Neighborhood association letter: We know the carrier followed FCC limits, and we're not claiming anyone has proven these towers cause illness. But no study has followed residents living next to one for thirty years. Until someone proves thirty-year exposure is harmless, the responsible assumption is that it isn't. We ask the city to deny the permit.

History of finance: During the tulip craze of 1636-37, contracts for rare bulbs traded for several times a craftsman's annual wage. Contemporary pamphlets argued that because everyone in Haarlem was buying bulbs, prices could only keep rising. Prices collapsed in February 1637, and many contracts were never honored. Historians still disagree about how widespread the losses were.

Hearing. REP. FALK: Ridgeway residents have complained about the smell for years, and I've read their letters. Commissioner, why did your office stop enforcing the emissions rules at the Ridgeway plant? COMMISSIONER: Our inspectors were there four times last year. REP. FALK: That's not an answer to my question.

Security review: The stadium's face-recognition system is genuinely impressive; in vendor testing it correctly identified wanted persons 99% of the time and misflagged only 1% of innocent faces. About 60,000 fans attended Sunday's game, and police believed around ten wanted individuals might be present. So when the system flagged the man in Section 114, the odds were overwhelmingly that police had found one of the ten. That made the decision to detain him reasonable, even if he turned out to be a mismatch.

District newsletter: Last fall we placed the 12 lowest-scoring elementary schools in the district into the Bright Start tutoring program. This spring, those schools improved by an average of 9 points, while the district as a whole improved by just 2. Since tutoring was the only new factor at those schools, the gain is strong evidence that the program works. We plan to expand it next year to the next 20 lowest-scoring schools.

Market column: Ken Abernathy's new forecast calls for a recession by spring, and it has gotten wide coverage. He has predicted a recession in each of the last six years, and none has occurred. That doesn't mean he's wrong this time. It does mean his forecasts haven't distinguished recession years from normal ones, so his call alone shouldn't move anyone's portfolio much.

Political analyst: Everyone is watching the reconciliation vote Thursday. Leadership says it has the numbers, and historically they usually do. I'd put about 30% on the bill failing, but closer to 45% on it failing because the moderates defect over the SALT provision. That story just fits everything we've seen this week.
Office party toast: People keep asking about my new diet. I'm on a seafood diet: I see food, and I eat it. Thank you all for coming, and please, nobody let me near the dessert table.

Budget office FAQ: Our revenue model has been used since 2015 and is reviewed by an outside panel each year. The state's official revenue estimates are generated by running this model with the governor's economic assumptions. The model's reliability is confirmed by how closely its projections track the state's official revenue estimates. Legislators can rely on it in this year's negotiations.

The family's claim that the 1791 council granted them the riverfront parcel has been repeated for two centuries. Our team read all 1,214 surviving council minutes for 1780-1800, a series with no gaps, in which every other land grant we can confirm from deeds and tax rolls is recorded within a month of the deed. No such grant appears. Given that the council recorded grants systematically and the series is complete, the absence is strong evidence that the grant was never made by the council, though it does not rule out a private sale.

Op-ed: The administration says interference in another country's elections is 'never acceptable,' and I agree that what Country Y did in our election was wrong. Yet the inspector general's report found that the agency's own democracy program paid for opposition campaign ads in Country Z in 2022. Either the principle has exceptions, which the administration should spell out, or that program broke it. A rule we apply only to rivals is not a rule other countries will respect.

Preservation op-ed: Walk through the old quarter and you'll see brick rowhouses from the 1850s still standing straight after 170 years, while some condos built in the 2000s already have leaking facades. The comparison is striking, and it shows up in city after city. Clearly, builders in the 1800s used better methods and materials than today's contractors. Our historic-district rules should require traditional construction for new infill.

Mayor's update: The street-repaving program finished two weeks early and under budget, and I want to thank the crews. The new LED streetlights went up in April, and by September burglaries had fallen 12%, so the lights are clearly paying for themselves in public safety. They also use 60% less electricity than the old sodium lamps. We'll finish the rollout next year.

Insurance adjuster: The policy covers theft only if the alarm was armed. Every time this system is armed, it writes an arm event to a tamper-proof audit log, and the manufacturer confirmed the log was functioning. The audit log shows no arm event at any time that night. So the alarm wasn't armed, and the claim falls outside the policy terms.

Council memo: We have spent $40 million, and that money is gone whichever way we vote. From here, finishing the transit center costs $9 million and is projected to generate $16 million in fares and leases over ten years. Stopping now costs $2 million in site cleanup and returns nothing. On the remaining numbers alone, finishing is the better choice.

Pharma press release: In our trial of 40,000 healthy adults, Clarivex cut the annual stroke rate from 2 per 10,000 to 1 per 10,000, a 50% reduction. Serious bleeding occurred in about 1 per 1,000 users per year. Halving your risk of stroke is a benefit no healthy adult should pass up. Talk to your doctor about Clarivex.

Quality report: The supplier's last shipment was tested before acceptance. We randomly selected 300 of the 12,000 units and found zero defects. With zero failures in a random sample of 300, we can be about 95% confident the lot's defect rate is below 1%, which is our contractual threshold. The lot is accepted.

Commissioner Brandt: Last year 112 people in this county died of overdoses; I knew four of them. The naloxone vending machines piloted in the next county dispensed 3,400 kits in a year, and their EMS logged 190 reversals using kits from the machines. The machines cost $14,000 each. I'm asking us to fund ten of them because the evidence says they save lives at low cost, not just because I'm grieving.

Recipe: Preheat the oven to 350 F. Whisk the eggs and sugar until pale, about three minutes. Fold in the flour in two additions, then pour into a buttered 9-inch pan. Bake 25 to 30 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean.

Blackjack seminar: Ten of the first fifteen cards dealt from this single deck were tens or face cards. Since the deck started with sixteen of them in fifty-two cards, only six remain among the thirty-seven undealt cards. So the next card is now less likely to be a ten-value card than at the start, about 16% instead of 31%. This works because cards aren't replaced, unlike spins of a roulette wheel.

Staff memo: The pool's operating deficit is projected at $120,000 next year. Option A would raise the fee to $45; Option B would keep the fee and cut weekend hours; Option C would seek a county grant. Cost and attendance estimates for each are in Appendix 2. Staff makes no recommendation at this stage.

Voter guide: The Labor Federation endorses only candidates with a consistent pro-worker voting record, so an endorsement is a reliable signal. Ms. Barrow didn't get the federation's endorsement this cycle, so voters shouldn't count on her to stand up for workers. Mr. Tate, who did get it, is the safer choice for working families.

Book review: The con man's pitch to the townspeople rests on a single line: 'Everybody on Main Street has already signed up.' The novel's pleasure lies in watching the bandwagon appeal work on one character after another. By the final chapter, the reader is wincing before each sale.

Community petition: Many of us have lost family members to cancer, and we believe the old landfill is responsible. We drew the boundary around the 14 households where neighbors reported cancers, and within that area the rate is three times the state average. That excess can't be a coincidence. We demand the county test the landfill and compensate affected families.

MODERATOR: Good evening and welcome to the second gubernatorial debate. Each candidate will have 90 seconds to answer and 60 seconds for rebuttal. The audience has agreed to hold applause until the end. A coin toss determined that Ms. Ferraro will answer first.

Op-ed: The new report finds that the state's voucher students scored lower in math after two years than similar students who stayed in public schools. The report was paid for by the state teachers' union. A report bankrolled by the teachers' union was never going to find anything else, so it tells us nothing about whether the schools work. Parents deserve real choices, not union talking points.

Travel column: Over a week in Ontario I visited three walk-in clinics with my nephew, who had a sprained wrist. At each one we waited more than four hours, and one clinic turned us away at closing. The staff were kind and clearly overworked. What I saw makes it clear the Canadian system fails patients who need timely care.

Op-ed: Drowning is the leading cause of death for American children aged one to four, and many of those deaths happen in home pools during a brief lapse in supervision. Imagine the forty seconds it takes to answer the door. Reviews of pool-fencing studies have found that four-sided isolation fencing substantially reduces child drowning compared with no fencing. That is why I support requiring four-sided fencing for new residential pools: it costs a few thousand dollars, and it addresses exactly the lapse every parent will eventually have.

Poll report: A survey of 1,203 registered voters, conducted Sept. 3-8, asked about Proposition 12. Fifty-four percent of respondents said they favor the measure, 41% oppose it and 5% are undecided. The margin of error is 3.6 points either way.

Defense closing: The only evidence placing my client at the warehouse at 9 p.m. is Ms. Darrow's account. She pleaded guilty to perjury in 2019, and her current plea agreement reduces her sentence only if her testimony 'substantially assists' the prosecution. No phone record, camera footage or second witness corroborates her. I am not asking you to conclude she is lying; I am asking you to recognize that her word alone cannot carry the state's burden beyond a reasonable doubt.

Loading plan: The freight elevator is rated for 3,000 kilograms. Each of the 14 crates is certified at no more than 180 kilograms, so together they weigh no more than 2,520 kilograms. Adding two handlers and a pallet jack keeps us under 2,800. We can move everything in one trip.

Letter to the editor: Daylight saving time was promoted in 1916 largely to save coal for the war effort. Nobody heats their homes with coal anymore. Since its original purpose is long gone, the practice has no justification today. Our state should stop changing the clocks.

IT recommendation: We should adopt the FHIR format for the patient-records exchange. Eighty-five percent of our hospital partners already send records in the FHIR format. I'm not claiming it is technically the best standard; I'm saying the value of an exchange format comes from compatibility, and choosing what most partners already use eliminates most of our conversion work.

Health news: Researchers surveyed 8,000 adults about how often they ate 40 common foods and tracked 12 health outcomes for five years. Among their findings, people who ate artichokes at least weekly reported 18% fewer migraines (p = 0.03). The study was large and carefully conducted, and the authors adjusted for age and income. The artichoke result was statistically significant, so readers prone to migraines may want to add artichokes to their diet.

Archive report: Researchers have asked whether they can trust the online catalog instead of requesting boxes in person. We checked 400 randomly chosen catalog entries against the physical boxes, and 397 matched. The three errors were misdated folders, not missing material. We therefore consider the catalog reliable for locating materials, though dates should be confirmed on the documents themselves.

Clinical note: Patient's symptoms raised concern for pertussis. The PCR panel, which detects this pathogen in over 99% of confirmed cases, came back negative twice. Combined with no known exposure, this makes pertussis unlikely, and we will stop prophylaxis for household contacts. If the cough persists beyond three weeks, we'll reconsider.

Shareholder letter: The board's vote to approve the merger was unanimous, and all seven directors were present. That means Director Okafor, who publicly criticized the deal in March, voted for it. Shareholders who relied on her March remarks should know her position changed, and we have asked her to explain why in the proxy statement.

Hospital comparison: Overall, 4.0% of surgical patients died at Mercy General last year, against 2.6% at Riverside. Broken down by risk, Mercy's mortality was 1.0% for low-risk patients versus Riverside's 1.5%, and 6.0% for high-risk patients versus Riverside's 8.0%. Mercy also treated far more high-risk cases, since it is the regional trauma center. Patients who want the best odds of surviving should choose Riverside.

Fund advertisement: The Apex Growth Fund has been managed by the same team since 2001. Measured from March 2009, the fund has returned 480%, so it plainly beats the market over the long run. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Fees are 1.2% a year.

Employee newsletter column: Nobody at headquarters will say it, but the signs are there. A company quietly preparing for layoffs freezes hiring well in advance. As of March, it has frozen all external hiring, so it's hard to avoid the conclusion that layoffs are on the way. If I were you, I'd update my resume.

Customer notice: We apologize for the outage that affected online banking from 2 to 5 p.m. on Tuesday. No account data was lost or exposed. Any late fees incurred during the outage will be refunded automatically within five business days.

Satire column: Breaking: scientists confirm that one hundred percent of people who drink water eventually die. Lawmakers are calling for an immediate ban, and bottled-water stocks plunged on the news. In related news, the columnist who wrote this has been asked to retake statistics.

Methods note: The survey-based method estimates local unemployment at 4.2% (plus or minus 0.9), and the claims-based method at 5.8% (plus or minus 0.6). Both are unbiased under their assumptions and their errors are independent. Weighting each estimate by the inverse of its variance gives 5.1%, with a narrower interval than either method alone. We report 5.1% as our headline figure.

Budget memo: The proposed 10-year tax abatement for the new distribution center looks like it costs $1.2 million. It doesn't. Section 9 of the 2018 development agreement requires the county to extend any abatement it grants to a competing facility to all three existing plants on the same terms. Counsel confirms the new center qualifies as competing. The realistic cost is therefore closer to $5 million, and the board should vote with that number in front of it.

I'm not arguing for the wetland option because it's 'natural.' The Corps' own 2023 study found that reconnecting the floodplain would store about 40,000 acre-feet during a 100-year flood, at roughly half the cost of raising the levee. It also avoids pushing more water onto towns downstream, which a higher levee would do. On cost and performance, the floodplain wins.

Homeowners association email: Last spring the creek reached the level engineers call the hundred-year flood, which flooded eight basements. The county has now proposed a flood-insurance surcharge for homes along the creek. Since we just had our hundred-year flood, the odds of another one in the next few decades are low, and the flood-insurance surcharge is a waste. Please sign the attached letter opposing it.

Analysis: Each party is attacking the other's farm bill for gutting conservation programs. According to the CBO, both bills cut conservation spending by about $6 billion over ten years. On that one dimension, the two bills are the same, so the criticism applies equally to both. They differ a lot elsewhere, especially on crop insurance and nutrition, and voters should judge those differences separately.

Election board ruling: A petition signature counts only if the signer is a registered voter in the district. The clerk counted Ms. Alvarez's signature, and that count was upheld in the audit. It follows that she was registered in the district when she signed, so the challenge to her residency fails.

Minutes, Parks Committee, Sept. 12: Meeting called to order at 6:03 p.m. Motion to approve the minutes of the August meeting passed 6-0. Staff presented the draft trail map; members requested a version showing accessible routes. Meeting adjourned at 7:15 p.m.

Radio debate. HOST: You said there's no evidence that guaranteed-income payments leave people's work effort intact. What would convince you? PRATT: Show me one randomized trial. GUEST: Here are three randomized trials, and none found significant declines in employment. PRATT: Those were in Scandinavia, and our labor market is different. Show me a study from an American city and then we'll talk. GUEST: The Stockton study... PRATT: One city isn't a nation.

Treasurer's report: Several members want to drop the two-signature requirement for checks because 'it's just how things were always done.' Before deciding, I looked up why we have it. The 1987 board minutes show the rule was adopted after a treasurer embezzled $300,000 through single-signature checks. That risk hasn't gone away, and our auditors say the rule is still our main control. I recommend keeping it, though we could raise the threshold to $1,000.

Public comment: The draft ordinance says no new structure may exceed the height of the tallest existing structure within 100 feet. On an empty lot, the tallest existing structure within 100 feet is nothing at all, so the rule as written forbids building anything there. I doubt the council intends to ban construction on every vacant parcel. The wording needs a floor, such as 'or 35 feet, whichever is greater.'

Rally speech: About 26 million Americans have no health insurance, and some studies find medical bills are a major factor in many personal bankruptcies. Single-payer would cover every one of them. Members who oppose this bill need to own that they're voting to keep 26 million people uninsured. There's no hiding from that vote.

The 1990s study that cleared the sweetener of any link to weight gain was funded by a beverage trade group. That alone wouldn't settle anything, since industry money funds plenty of good research. But internal emails released in litigation show the sponsor rewrote the primary outcome after interim results came in. A study whose endpoint was changed by an interested party after seeing the data shouldn't carry much weight until independent work replicates it.

Debate. CANDIDATE OSEI: Some charter schools in this state have underperformed, and the ones that have should face stronger oversight from the board. CANDIDATE LANGE: My opponent thinks charter schools are failing our kids. I've visited a dozen of them, and I've seen kids thriving who were lost in their old schools. I'm going to stand with those families.

Debate exchange. SEN. HALVORSEN: My opponent took $40,000 from the Clean Future PAC, and I've said many times that any candidate who takes that PAC's money cannot be trusted on energy policy. CHALLENGER RUIZ: I did take that money, and voters can judge it. But FEC filings show the senator's leadership committee accepted $55,000 from the same PAC last cycle. By her own stated rule, then, her committee is compromised too. Either she drops the rule or she applies it to herself; what she can't do is use it only against me.

Election analysis: In the last presidential race, the party carried 18 of the 20 states with the highest median household income and lost 17 of the 20 states with the lowest. The pattern has held for four cycles. Plainly, the party's base is wealthy voters. Its strategists should stop pretending to speak for the working class.

Supplement ad: ImmunoMax isn't a new fad. Over 14 million Americans have bought it, many of them every winter for a decade. Products that don't work don't keep 14 million customers coming back. Order now and get a second bottle free.

Lecture notes: Suppose a roulette wheel has landed on red eight times in a row, and a player bets on black because black is 'due.' This is the gambler's fallacy. Each spin is independent, so the chance of black on the next spin is the same as it always was, about 47% on an American wheel.

Testimony against HB 410: This bill would let employers in healthcare settings ask whether staff have received a flu shot. I understand the infection-control rationale. Once employers can ask whether you've been vaccinated, it is a short step to asking for your genetic test results and then to screening out anyone with a family history of illness. We should not open that door.
Office chat: My commute was so long this morning that I aged a decade and missed two elections. Anyway, I brought donuts. They're in the break room.

Homework, Unit 4: Identify the flaw in the following argument and explain what additional evidence would be needed. 'Since the new principal arrived, test scores have risen; therefore, the principal raised test scores.' Answers should be no more than 150 words.

Farm stand flyer: Our raw milk comes from grass-fed cows tested monthly for brucellosis and tuberculosis. Humans drank milk straight from the animal for thousands of years before pasteurization, which tells you which form our bodies are built for. Pasteurized milk is a 20th-century industrial product. Choose the milk your great-grandparents drank.

Science news: A study of 50,000 nurses found that those who drank two to three cups of coffee a day had slightly lower rates of type 2 diabetes over 20 years. The researchers stress that the study was observational and cannot show that coffee causes the difference. They plan a randomized trial next year.

Columnist's correction: In 2022 I predicted the rent-stabilization ordinance would cut new apartment permits by a third within two years. Permits fell 6%, about the same as in comparable cities without the ordinance. I was wrong about the size of the effect. I still think the exemption for new construction matters, and I'll watch whether permits change if it expires in 2027, but my original warning overstated the case.

Town hall: I'm a pharmacist, not a structural engineer, and I can't judge corrosion in a bridge deck myself. Three independent engineering firms inspected the span this summer, and all three rated the deck 'critical.' None of them was hired by the contractor who would do the repairs. When qualified people with no shared stake agree on a technical safety question, that's a good reason to close the bridge to trucks until repairs are done.

Testimony: Dr. Kessler's study concludes that the city's $18 minimum wage reduced teen employment by 6%. Her institute receives roughly a third of its budget from restaurant industry associations. Given who pays for her work, the council can set her paper aside. The rest of the research shows modest effects at most.

Incident report: The employee is accused of downloading the client file at 2 a.m. Our VPN records every authenticated session, the logs are hash-verified, and they show no session for that account between 1 a.m. and 3 a.m. The file server also shows no access from any device registered to her. We conclude the download did not come from her account, and we've widened the investigation.
Broadcast: Third and eleven, Martinez steps up and fires down the sideline. That pass was so perfect it should be hanging in the Louvre. First down at the 22, and the crowd is losing its mind.

Debate. MODERATOR: You've accused your opponent of wanting to eliminate the Department of Education. Is that fair? CANDIDATE PIERCE: At the March forum, she said, and I'm quoting the transcript, 'We should abolish the Department of Education, full stop.' She didn't say 'reform' or 'restructure'; she said abolish. So it's fair to ask her who would administer Pell Grants and special-education funding the day after.

Debate. SEN. WADE: I've proposed holding the growth of federal Medicaid spending to 3% a year instead of the projected 5%, so the program still grows, just more slowly. REP. CHEN: Senator Wade wants to cut Medicaid, plain and simple. Families in my district who rely on it for nursing-home care deserve to know that.

Prosecution memo: The statute makes it a crime to knowingly release a hazardous substance. The defense will argue that Mr. Pell didn't know the solvent was toxic. But it is a settled principle of our law that ignorance is no excuse. The defendant's ignorance of the solvent's toxicity is therefore no excuse. We should resist any jury instruction suggesting otherwise.

Policy memo: Retail pharmacies already require a second verification before dispensing high-alert drugs, even though a licensed prescriber wrote the order. We recommend the same independent double check for compounded pediatric IV doses on our wards. The drugs differ, the staff differ and the setting differs, but none of that touches the feature that justifies the double check: a single dosing error is potentially lethal and is reliably caught by an independent second reader. The added cost is about four minutes of pharmacist time per dose.

Column: The senator flew to the climate summit on a private jet, then lectured the rest of us about cutting our emissions. Three of his co-sponsors own homes with heated pools. If the people pushing these mandates don't believe the emergency is real enough to change their own behavior, the rest of us are entitled to doubt it too. The bill should be shelved.

Podcast: I've said for years that fiscal conservatives never support corporate subsidies. Then a listener pointed out that eleven self-described fiscal hawks voted for the chip-manufacturing subsidy. Anyone voting for this subsidy isn't a real fiscal conservative, whatever label they run under. So my point stands.

Floor statement: Members keep asking for a third way. Under the Antideficiency Act, if no appropriation is enacted by 11:59 p.m. Friday, these agencies must begin shutdown procedures; there is no third legal option. I'd welcome a better bill next month. Tonight, the choice in front of us is this stopgap or a shutdown, and I'm voting for the stopgap.

Campaign memo: Our polling is very good. Each of the five reform amendments polls between 58% and 66%, and the samples were large and representative. Since every one of the five amendments has majority support on its own, a ballot measure combining all five should pass easily. Let's bundle them into one measure and save on signature gathering.

Review: I used the budgeting app for a month, and it helped me notice how much I spend on takeout. That's just my experience; I'm one person with a fairly simple budget, and your mileage may vary. The subscription is $6 a month.

Product description: The kettle holds 1.7 liters and shuts off automatically when the water boils or the base runs dry. It has a removable limescale filter, a 360-degree swivel base and a 1,500-watt heating element. Available in black, white and sage.

Council hearing. COUNCILMEMBER YATES: Mr. Director, the state auditor's report, page 14, documents the contracts and the family relationship, and you haven't disputed either. Given that the audit found $2.3 million in no-bid contracts went to your brother-in-law's firm, who approved waiving the bidding requirement? DIRECTOR: The waiver was signed by my deputy under emergency authority.

Traffic study: Crashes fell 40% at the 25 intersections where cameras were installed. Because the sites were chosen for unusually high crash counts, part of that drop would have happened anyway as counts drift back toward normal. Using an empirical Bayes method with 200 similar high-crash intersections that didn't get cameras, we estimate the camera effect at about 15%. That smaller figure is the one the council should use.

Interview transcript. HOST: Thanks for joining us. What did you find most difficult about the transition from the Army to civilian work? And looking back, is there anything you wish someone had told you before you left?

The claim that '90% of workplace injuries happen in the first week on the job' has been repeated in safety trainings across the state. We traced it to a 2011 press release from a company that sells onboarding software. When reporters asked for the underlying survey, the company acknowledged that none existed. The figure may or may not be close to the truth, but as of now it has no evidential basis and shouldn't appear in official training materials.

Pollster's explainer: Our national survey interviewed 1,512 randomly selected adults, weighted to census benchmarks. Some readers will object that 1,500 people can't speak for 330 million. But a random sample's precision depends on how many people are in it, not on how big the population is; a well-stirred pot of soup can be judged by one spoonful. The margin of error here is about 2.5 points either way, which is why we report 52% support as a narrow majority rather than a landslide.

Consumer reporter: The manufacturer's spokesperson said last week that 'no Model R has ever experienced a total brake failure.' NHTSA complaint 11502271 describes exactly that, and an independent inspection of the vehicle confirmed a ruptured master-cylinder seal. One case doesn't tell us how common failures are. It does show the spokesperson's claim is false, and the company should correct it.

Trade memo: The proposal is meant to protect domestic manufacturing. Domestic manufacturers import about 60% of their components, so a 50% tariff on those components would raise their costs before it raised anyone else's. The Commission's 2019 analysis of similar tariffs found net job losses in downstream industries. We recommend targeting finished goods instead.

Wellness newsletter: Mainstream oncologists have been dismissive of the high-dose vitamin protocol. But last month Dr. Hans Mercer, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics for work on superconductors, signed an open letter saying the protocol 'shows clear promise.' When a Nobel laureate puts his name to a claim like this, the public should take the protocol seriously as a cancer treatment. Ask your doctor about it.

Science news: A new trial suggests the drug shortens cluster-headache attacks. Only 64 patients were enrolled, but they were randomized, the trial was double-blind, and the primary outcome was registered before enrollment began. Attack duration fell from a median of 52 to 21 minutes, a difference unlikely to arise by chance (p < 0.001), and an independent 2024 trial found a similar effect. The authors caution that a trial this size cannot detect rare side effects, which will require larger studies.

Product memo: After we launched the one-page checkout, conversion went up. Normally that alone would prove nothing. Users were randomly assigned to the old or new checkout, about 100,000 in each group. Conversion was 3.1% with the new page and 2.6% with the old, and the analysis plan was fixed before launch. The new checkout caused the increase, and we're rolling it out to everyone.
